archetype.name: Rebuilding (run-first, defense in freefall)
archetype.definition: A first-year staff at 1-9 with its starting quarterback on injured reserve, a defense that ranks last in efficiency, and a remaining schedule that offers few wins, so the rest of 2026 is about evaluating who belongs in the next version.

report.headline: A run-first team with no passing game and the league's least efficient defense.
report.take:
Jeff Hafley's first Dolphins team is a run-and-hide operation. Miami passes less than the situation calls for more than almost anyone, with a pass rate over expected of -8.6 that ranks 31st. When that works, as in the 217 rushing yards against Cincinnati or the 156 in the win at New York, they can stay in games. When it doesn't, nothing else carries the offense. They rank 31st in offensive success rate and 31st in points per game at 15.8, and the line gives up sacks at the third-worst rate in the league.

The defense is what sinks the season. Miami ranks 32nd in EPA allowed per play and 32nd in success rate allowed, and only three teams are worse on third down. The 13th-ranked yards allowed per game is misleading. Opponents don't pile up yards against this unit; they move the chains efficiently, hit explosives (deep-pass EPA allowed ranks 26th), and shorten the game, which leaves Miami 29th in time of possession despite a run-heavy plan. The perimeter corners hold up: opposing WR1s and WR2s score well under their usual output. Offenses have adjusted by sending targets to tight ends and third receivers, and Miami ranks dead last in EPA allowed to both roles.

The 1-9 record is a little crueler than the play. The point differential implies about two wins, and several losses (Minnesota, New England, Indianapolis) came down to one possession, so this is not a historically bad team. It is a bad one, though. Net EPA ranks 30th, and the decline didn't start this year: 2025 already brought a 27th-ranked net EPA and a 25th-ranked defense after a top-10 defense in 2024.

The quarterback situation is pushing it lower. Malik Willis started eight games before an abdominal injury put him on IR. In Kyle McCord's two starts the passing game produced -8.4 and -14.3 EPA, the second a 102-yard day in Buffalo. With Denver, Chicago, Green Bay and Buffalo still to come, the realistic win chances are this week's Jets rematch and the Week 16 Chargers game.

strengths.title: The run game can carry a day
strengths.body: Miami's blocking creates space early. The line ranks 3rd in yards before contact, and on its best days the offense leaned on that: 217 rushing yards against Cincinnati, and a balanced, efficient day at the Jets. It is boom-or-bust, though. The stuff rate also ranks 30th, so for every runway there is a run blown up in the backfield. It's real enough to keep games close against soft fronts, not enough to drive an offense week to week.

strengths.title: Perimeter corners erase top receivers
strengths.body: Opposing WR1s and WR2s both score well under their usual fantasy output against Miami, each ranking 3rd. Part of that is real coverage. Part of it is offenses choosing to look elsewhere, since wide receivers draw a smaller share of targets against Miami than the league norm. It is the one piece of the secondary to build around, and it depends on JuJu Brents' shoulder holding up.

strengths.title: Converts in short yardage
strengths.body: Miami ranks 10th in short-yardage conversion and goes for it on fourth down willingly. A downhill run scheme and an offense that leans on gap runs make this sustainable. It is a small edge, but it extends drives for an offense that struggles to string together positive plays any other way.

concerns.title: Last in defensive efficiency
concerns.body: This is the core flaw, not noise. Miami ranks last in EPA allowed and success rate allowed, 31st in pass EPA allowed, and 29th on third down. The rush is part of the cause, with pressure rate ranking 22nd. The bigger hole is the middle of the field, where tight ends and slot receivers have feasted. A light schedule didn't produce these numbers, and the slide began in 2025, so expect it to last.

concerns.title: The passing game has bottomed out
concerns.body: Even with Willis the pass offense ranked 26th in EPA. Since McCord took over, it has been worse: -8.4 passing EPA in Indianapolis and -14.3 in Buffalo. The line ranks 30th in sack rate and 28th in pressure rate allowed, and the slow time to throw points to a structure that can't win quickly. Until Willis returns (estimated mid-December, not guaranteed), defenses can sit on the run.

concerns.title: Middle of the field is wide open
concerns.body: Miami ranks 32nd in EPA allowed per play to opposing TE1s and to WR3s, and tight ends draw a larger share of targets against this defense than the league norm. That is how a unit that shuts down outside receivers still ranks last in efficiency: offenses have found the soft spot and keep attacking it.

trend.note: The middle of the season had life: the win at the Jets and a cover against New England. Since Willis went down, the passing game has collapsed, and the Buffalo loss was the offense's worst passing day of the year.

nextGame.headline: Home underdogs to the Jets, a team they already beat
nextGame.body:
Miami won the first meeting 28-25 in Week 7 with its best offensive game of the year: 156 rushing yards and a +10.1 passing EPA. The Book still makes the 3-8 Jets 3.5-point favorites in Miami with a 40.5 total, mostly because Willis isn't walking through the door. On paper this is two weak teams meeting. The Jets rank 23rd in net EPA to Miami's 30th, and their pass defense is nearly as leaky as Miami's: 30th in pass EPA allowed and 29th in EPA allowed on short throws. That gives McCord a quick-game path if the protection holds. The danger is that the Jets get home at the 5th-best sack rate, against a line that ranks 30th at keeping its quarterback upright.

Availability cuts both ways. Miami is without Willis (IR, abdomen), punter Bradley Pinion and receiver Jared Wayne, and Brents, a regular at corner, is day-to-day with a shoulder injury. The Jets are missing two of their most-used receivers, Isaiah Williams and Omar Cooper Jr. Geno Smith, who has started every game, will lean more on tight ends and backs. That is exactly where Miami's defense has been easiest to beat.

waysToWin.title: Quick game into the Jets' soft underneath
waysToWin.body: The Jets rank 29th in EPA allowed on short passes, and their defense has been generous to tight ends. Getting the ball out fast to Greg Dulcich and Malik Washington on underneath routes takes the Jets' pass rush out of the game and gives McCord easy completions. Malik Washington is the one to keep off a heavy diet, since the Jets hold WR1s well below their averages.

waysToWin.title: Replay the Week 7 script
waysToWin.body: Miami ran the ball well at the Jets and kept the passing game efficient off of it. The space the line creates before contact gives Ollie Gordon II room to set up manageable downs. A clean, low-turnover game with long drives keeps Miami's defense off the field and turns this into a one-possession fourth quarter.

waysToWin.title: Win it late against a shaky closer
waysToWin.body: The Jets have lost most of their close games and rank 31st in short-yardage conversion, so drives stall when they should finish. If Miami's defense can force a few third-and-shorts and fourth-and-shorts, the Jets may give away chances a better team would convert.

waysToLose.title: Jets' rush buries McCord
waysToLose.body: New York sacks quarterbacks at the 5th-best rate, and Miami allows them at the 3rd-worst. McCord has struggled even without heavy pressure. If Miami falls behind schedule and has to throw, this becomes Buffalo again: drives killed by sacks and negative plays, and the run game abandoned.

waysToLose.title: Geno works the middle
waysToLose.body: With two receivers out, the Jets will funnel targets to tight ends, backs and slot options, the roles Miami defends worst in the league. The Jets' offense ranks 9th in success rate, and against a defense that ranks 29th on third down, steady chain-moving drives can bleed the clock and put Miami out of reach.

waysToLose.title: Losing the hidden yards
waysToLose.body: Miami's special teams rank 28th in EPA per game, the Jets' are around average, and Miami's punter is out. In a game with a low total, a couple of short punts or a field-position swing can decide it.

nextGame.watch: How quickly McCord gets the ball out on early downs. Quick throws to the tight end and backs beat this Jets defense, while holding it hands the game to their pass rush.

restOfSeason.body:
The two winnable games left are this Jets rematch and the Week 16 Chargers game, against the league's worst offense. Denver, Chicago, Green Bay and Buffalo are all better than Miami on both sides of the ball, and New England's offense should find plenty against this defense. Some regression toward the point differential is fair, because Miami has lost more close games than a team this competitive usually does. The underlying efficiency, though, says the ceiling is a couple more wins, not a run.

The run game and the perimeter coverage should hold up. The passing offense depends on when Willis returns, and the IR estimate points to mid-December, which would give him a few games to steady things. The defense is the least likely piece to improve: it is last in the league against the run-and-pass mix, its middle-of-field coverage hasn't been fixed in ten games, and the decline dates back to 2025.
swingFactors: Timing and health of Willis' return from IR
Whether the defense can patch tight-end and slot coverage
Results in the Jets and Chargers games

confidence.note: Ten games of consistently bad defensive efficiency are telling, but the quarterback change splits the offensive sample.
